How to read this page (1 minute) — click to open

What it is. A live view of Sample Co.'s inventory plan for 112 products, laid out the way Sam recommended: Executive summary → Company by category → each channel (Marketplace, DTC, Retail) → Warehouse → Buy plan → Pricing & ROI → Scenarios. The main tabs always show the Excel workbook's numbers; to try different assumptions, use the Scenarios tab — nothing there changes the other tabs.

Actual, forecast and plan. Every line has five rows, actual first (Sam): Actual — from the records for closed months; open months show the forecast in grey until they close. Forecast — the planners' current view; for closed months it will show the forecast locked before the month (kept from October on). Plan — the target (the finance model until a plan is locked). Variance vs forecast and Variance vs plan — % and $ (or units). Money is shown to the nearest thousand ($241K); hover any number for the exact figure, click it for the detail.

Inventory lines
BOP inventory
Beginning of period — stock on hand at the start, at our unit cost.
Receipts
Stock received into our warehouses during the period: supplier deliveries, and on the channel tabs also stock moved in from another of our warehouses.
Returns & adjustments
Customer returns put back into stock, plus inventory count corrections.
COGS
Cost of goods sold — units sold × our unit cost.
Transfers
Stock moved between our warehouses and Amazon / Walmart. Not a sale; nets to zero for the company as a whole.
Other movements
In past months, the part of the change in stock the records don't explain — CareCorner ships from the 7720 warehouse, whose movements aren't in the history yet; stock in transit between warehouses; Walmart; timing. Zero in forecast months.
EOP inventory
End of period — stock at the close: BOP + receipts + returns & adjustments − COGS − transfers ± other movements.
Weeks of supply
How long the EOP stock lasts: EOP ÷ next month's COGS per week.
Turn
How many times a year the stock sells through: yearly COGS ÷ EOP.
On order
Open purchase orders arriving in the month, plus today's proposed order.
Open-to-buy
Receipts still to be placed: receipts needed minus what is already on order.
Sales lines
Net sales
What customers paid, after discounts.
Gross sales
The same units at full price.
Discounts / discount %
Gross minus net, and that as a share of gross.
AUR
Average unit retail — net sales per unit.
AOV
Average order value — net sales per order.
Aging
Days since received
How long stock has sat, oldest sold first. 0–120 days is the safe zone (about four turns a year).
Will pass 120 days
Stock that will cross 120 days before it sells at the current rate — act on it now.
Getting around

Click any number, card, bar or row for what's behind it; ‹ Back returns. Dotted-underlined terms and line names marked ⓘ explain themselves on hover (or click a line name). The full glossary is on the Glossary & method tab.

    Top-down vs bottom-up

    Top-down is the finance model (Jordan): cost of goods by channel and month. Bottom-up is this plan: every product's recent sales grown at the model's rate, summed up — or, once imported, Avery's and Sam's own SKU forecasts. The two are not meant to agree; the point is to see where and by how much they differ, then decide. To compare like with like, the bottom-up is restated at the finance model's cost basis using the ratio measured on the months both have actuals for (the model's cost line carries fees, freight and dropship that our purchase costs do not).

    Does the plan fit the finance model?

    The finance model implies a monthly purchase budget (cost of goods sold + change in planned inventory). This section takes off orders already placed and the order proposed today and shows what is left — the "open-to-buy". A positive number is not cash to spend: the model assumes we buy as fast as we sell, while the plan uses up the stock we already hold.

    How it works

    Inventory Open-to-Buy: sources and flow

    Answers one question per SKU: how much should we buy, and when? It combines stock, open purchase orders and demand from every channel into a weeks-on-hand view and a buy plan.

    Sources 7 systemsChannels DTC, marketplace, retailGrain SKU × month × warehouseOutput buy plan with MOQ flags

    How a refresh runs

    Pull

    Each source is read and stamped with its pull date.

    Reconcile

    Known data problems are listed on the page, with the judgement call made for each.

    Plan

    Demand, supply and targets roll up into weeks on hand and open-to-buy by month.

    Decide

    Ops reviews the buy plan; scenarios show what changes if demand moves.

    Where the numbers come from

    How the plan is calculated

    What to order (bottom-up). For each product, take its average monthly sales over the last three months in each channel (website sales from the warehouse records, Amazon from Amazon's own report, retail from customer orders in ERP, Walmart.com from Walmart's forecast). Scale each by how the finance model expects that channel to move. Compare with the stock we physically have plus orders already placed. If that stock would run below the target (supplier lead time + safety weeks) before a new delivery could arrive, propose an order, rounded up to what the supplier accepts, and check it against the supplier's minimum.

    Does it fit (top-down). The finance model implies a monthly purchase budget (cost of goods sold + change in planned inventory). Take off orders already placed and today's proposal; what's left is the "room". Separately, roll stock forward month by month and work out what still has to be ordered to stay at the stock level the model plans for.

    Everything on this page is recalculated from the same inputs as the Excel workbook; with the workbook's settings it reproduces the Excel numbers exactly.

    Sources and pull dates

      Known data problems (shown, not hidden)

      Judgement calls made in this version

      • The 7720 warehouse's stock is taken from the warehouse's own system (7K units); ERP shows 248K for it because transfers out were never deducted.
      • CareCorner orders count as sales from our own stock (they ship from 7720); Walmart store orders do not (Northwind ships them direct).
      • Amazon sales are counted in units, not listings (a 4-pack listing = 4 units). The previous version counted listings and understated Amazon by about 40%.
      • Walmart.com sales use Walmart's own forecast, because several listings were out of stock this summer.
      • Quantities still showing open on purchase orders already marked complete are ignored.
      • Orders below a supplier's minimum are flagged, not padded — topping up is an ops decision.
      • Walmart units under review are not counted as available.
      • Only seven lines come from the finance model: website orders, cost of goods for four channels, the change in planned inventory, and planned days of inventory. No revenue, cash or balances.
